title: the sound the universe hums
hookLine: a boy waits three days at Death's door and is given one word: om
tomorrow: the prayer you know by heart

cards: Om. A yoga class ends with it, and Hindu prayers begin with it. To see why, start with a boy who walked to Death's door.
His father, in a temper, shouted at him: I give you to Death. So Nachiketa went. Death wasn't home.
The boy waited at the door for three days without food, and when Death came back, ashamed to have kept a guest hungry, he offered him three wishes.

teach.b: For the third wish, Nachiketa asked the biggest question there is: what happens to us after we die? Death tried to talk him out of it. Take gold, he said.
Horses, kingdoms, a long life. The boy said no: all of that ends. So Death taught him, and at the heart of the teaching was one word.
The word every sacred text points to, Death said, is om.
This syllable is Brahman: the one reality underneath everything. That's the big idea inside the sound. For Hindus, om isn't a hum.
It's the name of the whole. Another short, old text says om is all of this, past, present and future, and hears four parts in it. A: waking, the world you can touch.
U: dreaming. M: deep, dreamless sleep. And the fourth has no sound.

teach.h: A, U, M — AND THE SILENCE.
teach.b: It's the silence after the m runs out, and the text calls it the self, at peace. That's why prayers, mantras and readings of scripture begin with om.
Before you ask for anything small, you name the whole. So the next time a room goes quiet before om, you'll know what's happening: everything is being named before anything is asked.

how: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

games.q: update: nani wants me to start the puja saturday by saying om three times. sam says om is a yoga thing?? wait, why do WE start with it
o: for us om is the sound of Brahman, the whole of everything. a prayer starts by naming the whole.
it's a warm-up hum so everyone's voices match.
it's a yoga word. hindus borrowed it from yoga classes.
games.why: Death told Nachiketa that om, the word every sacred text points to, is Brahman. Hindu prayers begin with it to name the whole before asking for anything.

games.q: what's inside the sound — tap the pairs.

s: an old Hindu text hears three sounds inside it, a, u and m, and a fourth part: the silence.
a whole Hindu text is built around om
a short text of twelve verses says om is all of this, then maps its sounds onto waking, dreaming and deep sleep.
om only belongs at the end of a class
the Bhagavad Gita says acts of offering, giving and discipline begin with om.

games.q: an old Hindu text gives a to waking, u to dreaming and m to deep sleep. what does it give the fourth part?
games.why: the fourth has no sound at all. the text calls it the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away.

games.q: build the sound in order: open, middle, closed.

practice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. Let it out as the sound, aloud or under your breath: a, u, m.
Let the m run out on its own, then stay a second in the quiet after it. That quiet is the fourth part.

wordCard.voice: Om. A, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it for the fourth. Second word on your strand.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the sacred syllable, written as one sign, with a, u and m inside it.

carryVoice: Your line: one sound, before words. Not a task. Something to notice the next time a room goes quiet before it begins. Day two, done.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1.1–1.2.16 (Nachiketa and Death; om as the word all the Vedas point to, and as Brahman)
